settings.foot: Customer reviews, in their own words. Individual experiences; results vary.

settings.body:
You read the labels and listened to the podcasts. You ended up with the names that keep coming up: NR, CoQ10, vitamin D3 with K2, a B complex, maybe zinc and resveratrol. You’ve been consistent for months. And you still can’t point at one pot and say “this is the one that’s working.”

That isn’t a discipline problem. It’s a design problem: doses you can’t see, ingredients sold one at a time, and no way to check any of it.

Here are seven reasons a cupboard of pots does less than it should, and why one daily protocol, two capsules with breakfast, can replace a good part of it.
settings.band_sub: Made in the UK · Every batch third-party tested · 90 days to decide

settings.title: You’ve been taking it for months. You still can’t tell what’s working. Here’s why.
settings.body:
A pot can list an ingredient without giving you a meaningful amount of it, and an all-in-one can list thirty ingredients at amounts too small to matter. The label has the name. You get a trace.

To take MUTO’s doses as separate products you’d need eleven pots on the kitchen side, every day. Nobody keeps that up for long, so the routine drifts, and then you blame yourself.

You’re not inconsistent. The routine was never built to be checked.
settings.answer: MUTO runs 300mg NR, the most allowed in Great Britain, and 150mg CoQ10, with every other dose printed on the label. Two capsules with breakfast.

settings.title: Your body doesn’t use nutrients one at a time.
settings.body:
Vitamin D3 and K2 belong together: both contribute to the maintenance of normal bones. The B vitamins work as a group: thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, B6 and B12 contribute to normal energy-yielding metabolism. Zinc and copper are balanced against each other.

Seven pots from seven brands were never designed to sit together. Nobody checked how they fit.
settings.answer: MUTO was built as one formula: NR alongside TMG, D3 alongside K2, a full B complex in active forms, and BioPerine® in the same two capsules. One design, one label, chosen by a PhD cell biologist.

settings.title: “Fine” isn’t the same as feeling like yourself.
settings.body:
The check-up comes back fine. On paper, nothing to see. In real life, the afternoons are slower, Sunday’s run is still in your legs on Wednesday, and your morning leans on coffee it didn’t used to.

Reference ranges exist to rule out deficiency, not to describe you at your best.

You’re not done yet. You just don’t want to settle for fine.

settings.text: MUTO is one daily routine for people who aren’t ready to settle for fine: two capsules with breakfast, every dose on the label, and 90 days to judge it on how your days feel.

settings.title: “Pixie dusting” is the industry’s open secret. Plenty of stacks are built on it.
settings.body:
Pixie dusting means listing an impressive ingredient at a dose too small to do anything. The ingredient is on the label. The dose is a trace. The label looks powerful; the formula is theatre.

It shows up in two main forms:

1. The proprietary blend. “Longevity blend: 2,500mg”, with no individual amounts. You can’t tell what’s doing the work, and neither can your GP or your AI. If a brand won’t show the milligrams, ask why.

2. The big-percentage multivitamin. 1,000% of a cheap water-soluble vitamin makes the label look generous. The ingredients that cost something are missing, or there in a pinch.
settings.answer: No blends and no pixie dust. All 19 ingredients and their doses are on the label, with the forms named: 300mg NR, 150mg CoQ10, zinc and copper as bisglycinate, B6 as P5P, B12 as methylcobalamin. Paste it into your AI, or ask Richie: he answers formula questions himself.

settings.title: At what point does this become ridiculous?
settings.body:
You know the moment. Sunday evening, refilling the pill organiser. NR, CoQ10, PQQ, D3 and K2, a B complex, zinc, resveratrol. Eleven pots. Ten minutes every morning. And a growing suspicion that you’ve become the supplement industry’s favourite customer.

It’s not your fault. It’s how the industry is set up.

The best-designed routine does nothing if you give up on it in month three because the ritual wore you down. Don’t abandon it. Replace it. The routine that counts is the one you keep every day, for years, without thinking.
settings.answer: Two capsules with breakfast, nothing to sort or time. Rate how you feel at 3pm today and, if you wear a watch, note a week of HRV, resting heart rate and sleep. Judge it at day 30 and day 90. If you don’t see a difference, you’re covered.
